issues.label: Subject-matter jurisdiction
issues.why: The court must have criminal jurisdiction over ORS 609.035 offenses and the alleged conduct.

issues.label: Venue
issues.why: The state must prove the offense occurred in the proper county or venue must otherwise be established.

issues.label: Valid charging instrument
issues.why: The accusatory instrument must sufficiently allege each statutory element and provide adequate notice.

issues.label: Correct statute version
issues.why: The court must apply ORS 609.035 as it existed at the time of the charged conduct, not the later-amended version.

issues.label: Identify governing subsection
issues.why: ORS 609.035 contains specific pathways/conditions; the court must determine which subsection(s) define the charged offense.

issues.label: Elements beyond reasonable doubt
issues.why: Each element (and any required circumstance/culpable mental state) must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

issues.label: Keeper status for each dog
issues.why: The state must prove defendant was the “keeper” of Moki and separately of Gyptian under the statutory definition.

issues.label: Dog identity and linkage
issues.why: The evidence must reliably identify the dogs involved and connect each dog to the injurious conduct.

issues.label: Domestic animal status
issues.why: The state must prove Baby Girl qualifies as a “domestic animal” within the statute’s scope.

issues.label: Physical injury to animal
issues.why: The state must prove “physical injury” occurred and was caused by the dog(s), not mere fear or minor contact.

issues.label: Causation by each dog
issues.why: For two counts, the court must decide whether each dog individually “caused” injury supporting separate convictions.

issues.label: No provocation element
issues.why: If “without provocation” is an element, the state must prove Baby Girl did not provoke the attack.

issues.label: Meaning of provocation
issues.why: The court must determine the legally correct definition/threshold for “provocation” (e.g., barking, nipping, biting through fence).

issues.label: Burden on provocation claim
issues.why: The court must decide whether provocation is an element the state disproves or an affirmative defense the defendant must prove.

issues.label: Location element interpretation
issues.why: The court must interpret the phrase “a location where defendant has no lawful right to exclude others” under ORS 609.035.

issues.label: Where incident occurred/began
issues.why: The court must fact-find whether the relevant conduct occurred/began on public path/outside fence versus inside defendant’s yard.

issues.label: Lawful right to exclude
issues.why: The court must determine whether defendant could lawfully exclude Gaul/Baby Girl from the precise area where the attack was initiated.

issues.label: Public way or easement status
issues.why: If the path is public or subject to an easement, that bears on exclusion rights and the location element.

issues.label: Trespass relevance
issues.why: If Baby Girl entered defendant’s property, the court must assess how that affects the exclusion-right/location element and provocation.

issues.label: Criminal negligence requirement
issues.why: If ORS 609.035 requires criminal negligence, the state must prove defendant failed to perceive a substantial unjustifiable risk.

issues.label: Gross deviation standard
issues.why: The court must apply ORS 161.085(10) to decide whether defendant’s conduct grossly deviated from reasonable care.

issues.label: Risk awareness and foreseeability
issues.why: The court must decide whether prior incidents, fencing condition, or dog behavior made the risk of attack substantial and foreseeable.

issues.label: Prior conviction admissibility
issues.why: The court must decide whether and for what purpose prior “public nuisance/potentially dangerous dog” convictions are admissible.

issues.label: Prior conviction as element
issues.why: If prior conviction is an element/trigger under the charged theory, it must be proven with competent evidence.

issues.label: Prior conviction proof method
issues.why: The court must ensure the prior conviction was proven by reliable records or admissible testimony, not improper character inference.

issues.label: Propensity evidence limits
issues.why: If prior acts are not elements, the court must avoid using them as impermissible propensity evidence.

issues.label: Separate counts double jeopardy
issues.why: The court must ensure two counts (one per dog) do not violate merger/double-jeopardy principles given one victim and one episode.

issues.label: Unit of prosecution
issues.why: The court must decide the legislature’s intended unit of prosecution (per dog, per victim animal, per incident, or per keeper conduct).

issues.label: Accomplice/collective causation
issues.why: If both dogs participated, the court must determine whether each dog’s conduct independently satisfies “caused physical injury.”

issues.label: Sufficiency of evidence
issues.why: The court must decide whether, viewed in the light most favorable to the state, evidence supports each element for each count.

issues.label: Conflicting eyewitness credibility
issues.why: The court must resolve credibility disputes among Gaul, Shoesmith, McCrery, and defendant on provocation and location.

issues.label: Bias and vantage considerations
issues.why: The court must consider potential bias, opportunity to observe, and consistency for each witness’s account.

issues.label: Physical evidence consistency
issues.why: The court must evaluate whether photos of injuries and fence damage corroborate either version (drag-through vs head-through).

issues.label: Chain/authentication of photos
issues.why: The court must ensure exhibits were properly authenticated and are what they purport to show.

issues.label: Causation of injuries scope
issues.why: The court must decide whether the injuries shown were caused during the alleged incident and meet the statute’s injury threshold.

issues.label: Defense theory of rescue
issues.why: The court must assess whether the dogs’ reaction to Zorro’s yelp/bite constitutes legally cognizable provocation or justification.

issues.label: Defense of property implications
issues.why: If defendant suggests a right to defend property/animals, the court must decide whether ORS 609.035 allows such a justification.

issues.label: Lawful presence of victim dog
issues.why: The court must decide whether Baby Girl’s lawful presence on a public path affects “without provocation” and location elements.

issues.label: Fence condition and duty
issues.why: The court must evaluate whether a makeshift barrier/broken fence reflects unreasonable risk-creation relevant to criminal negligence.

issues.label: Control and restraint obligations
issues.why: The court must consider what reasonable control measures were required (secure fencing, porch gate, supervision) under the circumstances.

issues.label: Timing of defendant intervention
issues.why: The court must assess whether defendant’s response time is relevant to negligence or causation under the charged statute.

issues.label: Pro se waiver validity
issues.why: The court must ensure defendant’s jury waiver (and any other waivers) were knowing, intelligent, and voluntary.

issues.label: Right to counsel advisement
issues.why: For a pro se defendant, the court must ensure proper advisement and waiver of counsel, if applicable in the record.

issues.label: Bench-trial impartiality
issues.why: The court must avoid reliance on inadmissible matters and maintain an impartial fact-finding role, especially with a pro se defendant.

issues.label: Due process notice of theory
issues.why: The state’s theory (elements such as prior conviction, location, provocation, mental state) must match what was charged and litigated.

issues.label: Statutory interpretation of ‘premises’
issues.why: The court must determine what constitutes “premises” for exclusion-right analysis (porch, yard, fence line, adjacent path).

issues.label: Boundary/fence-line legal significance
issues.why: The court must decide whether the relevant location is the outside of the picket fence, the fence itself, or inside the yard.

issues.label: Effect of dog dragged onto property
issues.why: The court must decide whether dragging Baby Girl into defendant’s yard changes the location element if the attack began outside.

issues.label: Mens rea per count
issues.why: The court must determine whether criminal negligence must be proven separately for each count/dog and whether evidence supports both.

issues.label: Findings adequacy for review
issues.why: The court should make findings sufficient to show it applied correct elements (provocation, location, mental state, per-count analysis).

issues.label: Potential merger at sentencing
issues.why: Even if guilty on two counts, the court must consider whether convictions merge or require separate sentences under Oregon law.

issues.label: Collateral consequences and classification
issues.why: The court may need to address any statutory mandatory consequences (e.g., dog restrictions) triggered by conviction under ORS chapter 609.
